primitives.name: Sensory Sign Relation
primitives.verbatim_quote: We shall then see that we are constantly selecting certain of our sensations as realities and degrading others to the status of signs of these.
primitives.assumptions: Selection of sensations as realities is probabilistic and context-dependent.
primitives.breakdown_regime: When sensory redundancy exceeds cognitive capacity, sign-reality mapping becomes ambiguous.

primitives.name: Joint Sensation Translocation
primitives.verbatim_quote: Thus the sensations to which our joints give rise when they rotate are signs of what, through a large number of other sensations, tactile and optical, we have come to know as the movement of the whole limb.
primitives.assumptions: Joint sensations are derived from multimodal sensory fusion.
primitives.breakdown_regime: Loss of proprioceptive feedback leads to mislocalization of joint activity.

layer2.mapping: Joint sensation J is a kernel function K(T,O) mapping tactile-optical inputs to perceived limb motion L.

reasoning_traces.think:
The core insight is that sensory translocation does not require a central projection point. Instead, sensations are mapped into a structured space where some act as signs for underlying realities. This is modeled as a Bayesian belief update: P(R|S_sign), where R represents the reality and S_sign is the sensory signal. The translocation occurs because the brain selects certain sensations as more salient or reliable indicators of reality. In the case of joint movement, the sensation J is not localized to a single point but is derived from a fusion of tactile and optical signals T and O, forming a kernel K(T,O) → L. Similarly, ground contact perception H is not directly sensed but inferred from V and T through a constraint function C(V,T) → G. These mappings form a dual structure: sensory input → sign → reality hypothesis. Failure modes arise when sensory redundancy or mismatch disrupts this isomorphism, leading to perceptual illusions or mislocalizations.
